scope.subject: Anatomy
scope.chapterTitle: Alimentary, Hepatobiliary systems, Pancreas and Spleen

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q001.takeaway: The oral cavity is bidermal: ectoderm from the stomatodeum and endoderm from the cranial foregut both contribute.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q001.displayText: The mouth is derived from both ectoderm and endoderm. Its ectodermal component comes from the stomatodeum, while its endodermal component comes from the cranial foregut. The buccopharyngeal membrane initially separates these two germ layers and disappears during the 4th week, after which the ectodermal and endodermal epithelia become continuous.

rationales.a: Endoderm contributes to the oral cavity, but the stomatodeal part is ectodermal, so endoderm alone is incomplete.
rationales.b: Mesoderm is not one of the two epithelial germ-layer sources tested for the mouth; the relevant pair is ectoderm plus endoderm.
rationales.d: Mesoderm does not add a third epithelial contribution to the oral cavity in this embryologic derivation; the tested origins are ectoderm and endoderm.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q002.takeaway: Embryonic folding incorporates yolk-sac endoderm into the embryo to form the primitive gut tube.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q002.displayText: The primitive gut is derived from endoderm. During cephalocaudal and lateral folding, part of the endodermal lining of the yolk sac is incorporated into the embryo as the primitive gut tube. Its cranial and caudal blind ends form the foregut and hindgut, while the intervening midgut remains temporarily connected to the yolk sac through the vitelline duct.

rationales.b: Ectoderm contributes to structures such as the stomatodeum and proctodeum, but it does not form the primitive gut tube.
rationales.c: The amniotic cavity surrounds the embryo and is not the germ-layer source of the primitive gut.
rationales.d: The intraembryonic coelom forms body cavities within lateral plate mesoderm; it does not give rise to the endodermal gut tube.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q003.takeaway: The duodenum straddles the foregut–midgut junction: proximal duodenum is foregut-derived and distal duodenum is midgut-derived.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q003.displayText: The duodenum develops from both the caudal foregut and the cranial midgut. This dual origin explains why the duodenum lies at the transition between foregut and midgut territories. The foregut also gives rise to the pharynx, esophagus, stomach, liver, gallbladder and pancreas, whereas the midgut continues distally through the small intestine, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.
emphasis: proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon

rationales.a: Foregut alone accounts only for the proximal part of the duodenum; the distal part is derived from midgut.
rationales.b: The hindgut does not contribute to the duodenum; its intestinal derivatives begin at the distal one-third of the transverse colon.
rationales.d: Midgut alone accounts only for the distal duodenum; the proximal duodenum is foregut-derived.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q004.takeaway: Gut arterial territories mirror embryologic origin: celiac trunk supplies foregut, SMA supplies midgut, and IMA supplies hindgut.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q004.displayText: Foregut derivatives of the digestive system are supplied by the celiac trunk. The corresponding embryologic arterial territories are celiac trunk for foregut, superior mesenteric artery for midgut, and inferior mesenteric artery for hindgut. This foregut–celiac, midgut–SMA and hindgut–IMA pairing is the key discriminator.

rationales.b: The superior mesenteric artery is the principal arterial supply of midgut derivatives, not foregut derivatives.
rationales.c: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies hindgut derivatives rather than the foregut.
rationales.d: The abdominal aorta is the parent vessel from which these unpaired branches arise, but the specific foregut artery is the celiac trunk.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q005.takeaway: The cecal bud arises from the caudal/post-arterial limb of the midgut loop and forms the cecum and appendix.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q005.displayText: The cecal bud develops as a diverticulum from the post-arterial, or caudal, segment of the midgut loop. Its proximal part enlarges to form the cecum, while its narrow distal part forms the appendix. More broadly, the cranial limb of the midgut loop forms the jejunum and upper ileum, whereas the caudal limb forms the lower ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

rationales.a: The pre-arterial/cranial limb mainly forms jejunum and upper ileum; the cecal bud arises from the post-arterial limb.
rationales.c: There is no hindgut loop giving rise to the cecal bud; the cecum and appendix are midgut derivatives.
rationales.d: The cecal bud is specifically a post-arterial midgut structure, not a post-arterial hindgut structure.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q006.takeaway: The midgut rotates a total of 270° counterclockwise around the superior mesenteric artery.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q006.displayText: The midgut loop undergoes a total 270° counterclockwise rotation around the superior mesenteric artery. Rotation begins during physiologic herniation and is completed as the bowel returns to the abdomen. The source describes about 90° of rotation in association with return from the umbilical hernia and the remaining 180° after the loops are in the abdominal cavity. The proximal jejunum returns first and the cecal bud returns last.

rationales.b: A total of 180° is insufficient; normal midgut rotation totals 270° around the SMA axis.
rationales.c: The magnitude is correct but the direction is wrong: normal rotation is counterclockwise, not clockwise, when viewed from the front.
rationales.d: Both the magnitude and direction are wrong; the normal total is 270° counterclockwise.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q007.takeaway: Persistence of the vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct classically produces a Meckel diverticulum of the ileum.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q007.displayText: Meckel diverticulum results from persistence of a portion of the vitellointestinal duct, the embryonic connection between the midgut and yolk sac. The persistent remnant forms an ileal outpouching and is present in about 2% of the population. Other patterns of incomplete vitellointestinal-duct obliteration can occur, but the classic persistent remnant tested here is Meckel diverticulum.

rationales.a: Omphalocele results from failure of physiologically herniated bowel to return to the abdomen, not persistence of the vitellointestinal duct.
rationales.b: Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical abdominal-wall defect with uncovered bowel and is not a vitellointestinal-duct remnant.
rationales.d: The urachus is derived from the allantoic/bladder connection; it is embryologically distinct from the vitellointestinal duct.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q008.takeaway: The cloaca contributes to distal rectum/upper anal canal and the urogenital sinus, whereas the sigmoid colon is a more proximal hindgut derivative.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q008.displayText: The sigmoid colon does not develop from the endodermal cloaca. The cloaca is the caudal end of the hindgut and is divided by the urorectal septum into an anterior primitive urogenital sinus and a posterior primitive rectum. The urogenital sinus contributes to the urinary bladder and urethra, while the posterior compartment contributes to the lower rectum and upper anal canal. The sigmoid colon develops from hindgut proximal to the cloacal region.
emphasis: sigmoid colon does not develop from the endodermal cloaca
lower rectum and upper anal canal

rationales.a: The distal/lower part of the rectum receives a cloacal contribution through the posterior primitive rectum, so rectum is not the exception.
rationales.b: The upper anal canal is endodermal and derives from the hindgut/cloacal compartment; only the lower anal canal is ectodermal from the proctodeum.
rationales.d: Most of the urinary bladder develops from the vesical part of the primitive urogenital sinus, which is derived from the anterior cloaca.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q009.takeaway: Anal agenesis with a perineal fistula points to abnormal cloacal partitioning by the urorectal septum, not simple persistence of the anal membrane.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q009.displayText: Incomplete separation of the cloaca by the urorectal septum can produce anal agenesis with an abnormal fistulous communication. Normally the urorectal septum divides the cloaca into urogenital and anorectal compartments. The upper anal canal is endodermal from the hindgut, the lower anal canal is ectodermal from the proctodeum, and the intervening anal membrane normally breaks down around the 9th week. A perineal fistula therefore favors a partitioning defect rather than an isolated failure of anal-membrane perforation.
emphasis: anal membrane normally breaks down around the 9th week

rationales.a: Degeneration of the anal membrane is a normal event that establishes continuity of the anal canal; it does not cause anal agenesis with a fistula.
rationales.b: Failure of anal-membrane perforation can cause an imperforate anus, but the associated perineal fistula in this stem points to abnormal cloacal partitioning.
rationales.d: Failure of colonic recanalization would produce an intestinal atresia/stenosis pattern, not anal agenesis with a perineal fistula.

marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q010.takeaway: Omphalocele is failure of physiologically herniated midgut to return, leaving membrane-covered viscera within a central umbilical defect.
marrow__ANAT_CH07_Q010.displayText: Failure of the physiologically herniated intestinal loops to return to the abdominal cavity produces an omphalocele (exomphalos). The herniated viscera protrude through a broad umbilical defect and remain covered by a membranous sac that includes amnion. This distinguishes omphalocele from gastroschisis, in which bowel protrudes through a usually right-sided paraumbilical defect without a covering sac. The source stem places the failed return by the 11th week, while its explanation describes failure during the 6th–10th-week return interval; the key embryologic defect is the same failure of midgut return.
emphasis: right-sided paraumbilical defect without a covering sac

rationales.b: Gastroschisis is usually a right paraumbilical wall defect with exposed bowel and no covering sac; it is not caused by persistence of physiologic midgut herniation.
rationales.c: Bladder exstrophy reflects failure of lower ventral abdominal-wall/cloacal-region development, not failure of the midgut loops to return.
rationales.d: An ileal (Meckel) diverticulum is a vitellointestinal-duct remnant and is unrelated to persistence of physiologic midgut herniation.
